what: Disney's Audio-Animatronic Abraham Lincoln shown in 'Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln' at the Illinois pavilion, 1964 New York World's Fair

sources.title: Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln
sources.quote: Originally created by Walt Disney for the State of Illinois pavilion at the 1964 New York World's Fair

note: A figure of one particular (dead) person; it is a likeness rather than a verified exact double. Rejected as later: Repliee Q1Expo (2005) and Geminoid HI-1 (2006, Ishiguro's copy of himself, teleoperated). Earlier wax or automaton portraits not found as robots.

what: Whirlpool demonstrated a track-following robotic floor sweeper concept (Donald Moore's 1957 patent) at the American National Exhibition in Moscow

sources.title: Robotic vacuum cleaner
sources.quote: Whirlpool demonstrated the concept at the 1959 American National Exhibition but did not bring it to market.

note: Follows a track under the floor, so only a loose fit to 'on its own'. Later: MowBot 1969, Electrolux Trilobite 1996, Roomba 2002. Heinlein 1956 was fiction.

what: MowBot, autonomous robotic lawn mower patented by S. Lawrence Bellinger, sold for about $800

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger having many features of today's most popular products.

note: No earlier robot mower or vacuum on sale found in the pages read. Trilobite (1996) and Roomba (2002) are later. Whether MowBot was truly autonomous rests on this one source.

what: Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated dispenser of water for ablutions in Mechanics

sources.title: Hero of Alexandria
sources.quote: A vending machine that dispensed a set amount of water for ablutions when a coin was introduced via a slot on the top of the machine.

note: Date is Hero's floruit (c. AD 62), not a dated event; a described design, no record that it was built. Nothing earlier found.

what: Coin-operated brass tobacco dispensers operated in English taverns

sources.title: Vending machine
sources.quote: Coin-operated machines that dispensed tobacco were being operated as early as 1615 in the taverns of England.

note: Considered and rejected as later: Carlile newspaper machine 1822, Denham stamp machine 1867, Everitt postcard machine 1883, Quisisana automat Berlin 1895, Horn & Hardart Philadelphia 1902. The 1615 claim is from one reference page without a primary source.

what: Coin-operated postcard and stationery machines, introduced in London in 1883, became widespread at railway stations and post offices

sources.title: Vending machine
sources.quote: soon became a widespread feature at railway stations and post offices

note: Exact year of becoming common not given; 1883 is the introduction. Automats became popular in New York after 1912 (Horn & Hardart).

what: W. Grey Walter's tortoise robots Elmer and Elsie in Bristol, built 1948-1949

sources.title: Grey Walter
sources.quote: Elmer and Elsie, were constructed between 1948 and 1949

note: Earlier candidates: Hammond and Miessner's Electric Dog (c. 1912, a light-seeking prop; the page read gives no date for it); Vaucanson's duck (1739, page read gives wrong date); ancient and medieval animal automata (Hellenistic, Al-Jazari). Not dated from sources I could fetch, so 1948 may be too late.

what: Tiger Electronics released the Furby, an electronic robotic toy creature, in October 1998
note: Furby is a creature toy rather than a dog or cat, but sold as a pet-like robot. Considered: AIBO ERS-110 sales 1 June 1999 (later, higher fidelity as robot dog); Teddy Ruxpin 1985 (talking animated bear, not pet-like).

what: Furby sold 14 million units in 1999 after 1.8 million in 1998

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: with 1.8 million sold in 1998 and 14 million in 1999

note: Toy-store scale adoption. AIBO sold only thousands in 1999.

what: Sony introduced the first consumer AIBO robot dog (ERS-110)

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: The first consumer model was introduced on 11 May 1999 and was followed by updated generations.

note: Companionship fit is loose (AIBO means pal). Paro was designed from 1993 but first shown to the public in late 2001 per the page read (first pass said 1998, not confirmed). No romance or sex robot (RealDoll 1997 is a doll, not a robot; Realbotix 2018) earlier.

what: AIBO ERS-110 went on sale and sold out in 20 minutes

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: Sales began on 1 June 1999 and sold out via the Internet in 20 minutes.

note: Paro handmade versions sold from 2004 are later.

what: US Navy testing of pre-production Mark 24 'FIDO' acoustic homing torpedoes, which steer themselves onto a target

sources.title: Mark 24 mine
sources.quote: Testing of the pre-production prototypes continued into December 1942

note: Date is when prototype tests were still running; the first successful test date is not given. Naval and land mines considered and rejected: they do not find targets. Phalanx CIWS (OT&E 1977) is later.

what: Mark 24 mine entered Allied service in March 1943; first U-boat kills claimed in May 1943

sources.title: Mark 24 mine
sources.quote: Two engagements in May 1943 have a claim for the first U-boat sunk by FIDO.

note: German G7es acoustic torpedo also entered service in 1943. Kargu-2 (2020) is far later.

what: Lt. John Dumaresq, Royal Navy, invented the Dumaresq, a mechanical analog computer relating own-ship and target motion for gunnery

sources.title: Dumaresq
sources.quote: The Dumaresq is a mechanical calculating device invented around 1902 by Lieutenant John Dumaresq of the Royal Navy.

note: It computes relative motion (range rate), not full aim; Dreyer Table and Ford Rangekeeper (1916) came later. Missile guidance (V-1, V-2, Fritz X, 1940s) not searched and later in any case.

what: Mechanical fire-control aids such as the Dumaresq began to be available to the Royal Navy around 1905

sources.title: Fire-control system
sources.quote: Around 1905, mechanical fire control aids began to become available

note: Dumaresq patented August 1904 and about 1000 bought by 1913. Rangekeeper 1916 (first pass) is later.

what: SAGE air-defence computers (IBM AN/FSQ-7) became operational in the late 1950s

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: SAGE became operational in the late 1950s and early 1960s

note: Air-defence tracking, not war planning. Earlier candidates not verifiable here: Army Operations Research Office computer war-game and combat simulations (Air Defense Simulation 1948, Carmonette 1953) seen only in search summaries; ORO founded 1948. Likely earlier events exist.

what: Knightscope shipped its first autonomous security patrol robot

sources.title: Knightscope
sources.quote: Knightscope shipped their first robot in 2015.

note: Almost certainly too late. Earlier: Denning Sentry (mid-1980s), ROBART I (c. 1982), PROWLER armed sentry (developed from 1983); I could not fetch usable dated sources for them.

what: Walgreens installed a Kiva mobile-robot fulfilment system at Mount Vernon, Illinois

sources.title: Amazon Robotics
sources.quote: Walgreens installed one at its distribution center in Mount Vernon, Illinois, in 2007

note: Too late probably: AGV fleets under central computer traffic control existed in the 1970s (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74 seen only in search summaries, central control not confirmed). Staples 2006 not confirmed.

what: Key-wound spring-driven clockwork monk, now in the Smithsonian, possibly dating as early as 1560

sources.title: Automaton
sources.quote: The monk is driven by a key-wound spring and walks the path of a square, striking his chest

note: Date is 'possibly'. Earlier automata rejected on mechanism (water, weights, pneumatics): Hellenistic (Ktesibios, Hero), Al-Jazari 1206, Strasbourg clock figures (14th c.). Leonardo's mechanical lion and knight (c. 1495-1515) may have been spring or weight driven; unclear.

concept_note: First pass had Geminoid 2006 (teleoperated); found Disney Lincoln 1964 as a weak earlier likeness. No practical use or mass adoption.
No general-purpose housework robot has been in real use; vacuums and mowers are covered by robot-vacuum-mower. No milestones.
Added 1959 Whirlpool demonstration (loose fit); kept 1969 MowBot. Roomba 2002 'commercially successful' but no source for routine use, so no mass_adoption.
No milestone: could not fetch a source for Savioke 2014 or earlier HelpMate (hospital courier, c. 1988-91 per search summaries only), so both are dropped, not refuted.
Moved much earlier: Hero (AD 62, described only), tobacco boxes 1615 (single source), postcard machines 1883. First pass 1895 Quisisana was an automat restaurant.
No milestone: nothing found that actually looks after children; toys and tele-presence do not fit.

First pass Paro 1998/2005 not confirmed (page says exhibited 2001, sold from 2004); used AIBO 1999 as an earlier companion-type robot. No sex or romance robot meets the definition before 2018; no mass adoption.
Kept Walter 1948 (low, earlier animal automata and Electric Dog exist but undated in my sources); practical use moved to Furby 1998 (AIBO 1999 later); added Furby mass adoption 1999.
First pass Al-Jazari 1206 was water-driven; replaced by spring-driven monk (c. 1560) with low confidence. Practical use and mass adoption not established.
Kept Knightscope 2015 as low confidence; earlier 1980s sentries could not be sourced.
Moved from Kargu-2 2020 to the 1943 Mark 24 acoustic homing torpedo; Phalanx (tested 1977) also precedes 2020.
Moved from 1916 Rangekeeper to the Dumaresq (1902) and 1905 fleet use; missile guidance not checked.
Kept SAGE (1958) at low confidence; computer war-game simulations from 1948-55 probably earlier but unsourced here.
Replaced Staples 2006 with Walgreens 2007 (sourced); earlier central-computer AGV fleets likely exist, unsourced.
No milestone: no machine has built working copies of itself from raw materials without help.

_tools: page_text worked for Wikipedia pages only; other hosts (army.mil, kollmorgen, aiwiki, ntrs) timed out or were refused by the proxy; chronam and WebFetch not used; Savioke, HelpMate, Hospital_robot, Relay Wikipedia pages returned empty.
